Title_wuva: Alabama senior seeks out new challenges in path to med school
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 Digital Reporter Candace Johnson Rising University of Alabama senior Kyra Berger is set to study abroad in Denmark to work towards medical school. Chemical engineering major Kyra Berger started a research position last year in UA engineering professor Shreyas Rao's lab. There, she began to learn to conduct experiments and was introduced to undergraduate research. She initially struggled to comprehend the difficult tasks that was unfamiliar to her. "It was all very confusing," she said. Despite this setback, she persevered and continued to improve. Berger took upper-level courses in genetics and biochemistry while simultaneously studying for the MCAT. "There were certain things about the immune system that I was learning for the MCAT and had to understand when I thought, "Wow, I'm researching this right now,'" she said. "Then I'd go to the lab, where I would have to add a certain chemical to help separate cells, and I would remember learning in class about what that chemical does." "I understood what I was doing and why." The Mountain Brook native is set to take her educational journey a step further by making an unexpected stop. Berger will study at the Technical University of Denmark to participate in a monthlong four-hour course. There, she will conduct experiments and write formal lab reports. "I usually spend summers focused on pre-med, either shadowing someone or working in Dr. Rao's lab," said Berger. "But there are amazing faculty and plenty of equipment to use (at DTU) that I'm excited about." Rao said students must be dedicated when it comes to taking the class. Students must be "motivated, driven and embrace different viewpoints in an interdisciplinary environment," said Rao. "Especially those who want to go to graduate school or medical school," he added. "They can work toward finding answers, publish results and highlight their research during their interviews." Berger and one of Rao's post-doc researchers are working to understand how different cell types contribute to the progression of brain tumors. "I like the size of the lab and how everyone is close and working together, but I can also be very independent in the lab," Berger said. "Dr. Rao really wants us to learn and do our own work; we're not just standing to the side and assisting." Upon high school graduation, Berger received the Presidential Scholarship, UA's top merit scholarship, and the Dr. E. Gaylon McCollough Endowed Scholarship which is awarded to outstanding prospective medical students. Berger said she was inspired by her AP chemistry teacher Bryan Rosensteil who persuaded her to pursue a degree in chemical engineering. "Rosensteil knew that I loved being creative and that I loved physics," said Berger. "I liked working hard, being challenged and being outside of my comfort zone." Chemical engineering is widely viewed as the most difficult undergraduate engineering program. When accompanied with pre-med courses, the pressure can add up. "I questioned if I could keep this up," she said. "But I was determined to stick it out." Fortunately, she was not alone and had a support system by her side. Berger found support from her professors who assisted in her coursework, as a result, she was named "Outstanding Sophomore" by the UA College of Engineering. She was even able to have the opportunity presented to her by a fellow Mountain Brook grad. Department chair for chemical and biological engineering Dr. Heath Turner introduced the study abroad to Berger and her parents. Berger said she's grateful for the opportunities that UA has provided to her. "Even though I'm a chem-E major, I've been guided completely through every step of my pre-med process," she said. "Everyone is looking out for us. I've met so many amazing people, and I can't thank UA enough."

Title_wuva: Look before you lock: Don't leave children in a hot car
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Zoe Blair The temperature inside a car can rise 19 degrees in just 10 minutes when it's stationary and turned off. Those 10 minutes could be fatal for someone stuck inside. "When cars are parked, they warm up rather quickly," said Tuscaloosa Safe Kids Coordinator Charlene Wilkinson. "We've seen the temperature in the car get up to 40 degrees hotter than the outside temperature." While adults can usually find a way out of a car that hot, toddlers and infants can't. Wilkinson said that makes it extremely important to look before you lock your car. "Children's temperatures tend to rise three to five times faster than ours, so this is a critical time for them," Wilkinson said. DCH Regional Medical Center Emergency Department Director Dr. Elwin Crawford said young children face the highest risk of heat emergencies. "You know, anytime it gets this hot and you're outside with children, especially infants and young children, they are much more prone to heat emergencies than adults and older kids," Crawford said. You can create reminders for yourself when you get in the car to help you remember to get your child from the backseat. Put your phone, purse, or wallet in the backseat if you typically grab that before you get out. Wilkinson also encourages you to put one of your child's toys in the front seat as a reminder. Last year, 36 children died in the United States because they were trapped in a hot car. Two of those children were from Alabama. "That's two too many," Wilkinson said. If your child gets locked in a hot car or you see a child locked in a car, Wilkinson and Crawford encourage you to call 911 immediately.
Title_wvtm: Doctors urging people to stay hydrated during dangerous summer heat
Description_wvtm:
Doctors withAmerican Family Careare urging people to stay hydrated as we head into the weekend and brace for the heat.
Many patients are coming into the clinics with cramps, heat exhaustion, and some feeling lightheaded, according to Chief Medical Officer Dr. LouAnne Giangreco. She is encouraging people to take heat-related illnesses seriously.
"We think we can power through some of these times without making sure we are taking frequent breaks, that we are not taking breaks outside in the heat; making sure we have great sun protection as well if we are in the sun and the heat. Make sure we have appropriate sun protection," Giangreco said.
>>CHECK WEATHERWarmest days of the year: Alabama is heating up just in time for Father's Day
According to theCenters for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC),people who are at the highest risk of heat illnesses include those aged 65 and older, children younger than 2, and people with chronic diseases or mental illness.
Doctors at AFC are encouraging people to ensure they have access to fluids, bottles of water, and fans to battle the heat.
When it comes to heat exhaustion, here are some symptoms to watch out for, according to the CDC: heavy sweating, clammy skin, fast or weak pulse, cramps, and nausea. If you feel like you could be having a heat stroke, seek medical attention.

Title_wuva: Alabama seeking foster care homes for older adults in need
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 Digital Reporter Candace Johnson June 15 wasWorld Elder Abuse Awareness Day, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey is using that day as a springboard to spread awareness of how many older adults there are in the state who need help. One major way older adults can get help in their communities is through an adult foster home. Just like children who need foster homes, adults in foster care are a vulnerable demographic who may well thrive in a home environment instead of a group care setting. TheAlabama Department of Human Resources' Adult Protective Servicesprogram is focused on keeping older adults from financial, emotional or physical abuse. In fiscal year 2023, DHR got more than 12,000 reports of elder abuse or neglect. Warning signs of suspected adult abuse include: Qualified and caring adult foster homes are one solution to this problem. Instead of staying in an abusive home, older adults can be placed with families who want to help them thrive. DHR's mission is recruiting at least one adult foster home in each of Alabama's 67 counties. "The rise in elder abuse and neglect over the last decade has been disheartening, but we have also seen so many individuals step up to provide loving, caring homes for many of Alabama's aging individuals," said Alabama DHR Commissioner Nancy Buckner. "Becoming an adult foster care provider is both helpful for the adult in need and incredibly rewarding for the person opening their home." The Adult Foster Care program serves adults who are capable of living in a safe home environment but may need additional assistance from time to time. "We are proud to partner with DHR to find the absolute best services and care for seniors in need," saidAlabama Department of Senior ServicesCommissioner Jean Brown. "Adult Foster Care is a life-changing experience for everyone involved and can brighten the lives of some of Alabama's most vulnerable residents." Adult foster care provider Beth Nelson in Elmore County said providing this service has changed her life for the better. "I've had an adult foster in my home for nearly 16 years and it has enriched both of our lives," said Nelson. "I don't know what would have happened to him had I not taken him in back then. We've become family and do everything together." If you're interested in finding out how to qualify or what being an adult foster home entails, you can learn moreright here. Title_wuva: Children's of Alabama celebrates 113th birthday this week
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 Digital Reporter Candace Johnson Children's of Alabamain Birmingham, Alabama's only free-standing pediatric hospital, celebrated its 113th birthday June 17. "We are celebrating another year of delivering world-class healthcare services to families from across Alabama and the Southeast," said Children's CEO and President Tom Shufflebarger. "We are looking forward to celebrating more milestones as we continue to grow and improve healthcare for our patients." Throughout the previous year, Children's has provided care to more than 680,000 patients and admitted more than 16,000 patients. Several of the Children's of Alabama's subspecialties have been listed in theU.S. News and World Report's Best Children's Hospital editions. In celebration of the birthday, the hospital is hosting its fifth annual Celebrate Campaign, honoring patients, families and community partners for an entire week. Title_wuva: Everything must go: Buddy's restaurant hosting equipment sale after closure
Description_wuva: Buddy's Rib and Steak,a staple of Northport's restaurant scene,closed its doors Monday June 10, having served the people of West Alabama for 45 years.Â  The restaurant's equipment is now being sold to the public. Current Buddy's owner Phillip Guy was there for the sale. While there were some casual lookers, he said they also had some serious buyers. "Well, a little bit of everything is for sale," said Guy. "We still have some pictures, booths and tables and kitchen equipment for sale. I already sold one of our big freezers today which was good." The three-day sale started Monday, June 17. All the furnishings, equipment and memorabilia will be sold. Items are being sold as-is and cash only. The business needs to be cleared out by close of business Wednesday, June 19. Guy said the building has already been sold and will reopen as another restaurant. *
Title_wvtm: Iconic Northport restaurant set to close after nearly five decades
Description_wvtm:
A Northport landmark since the 1970s is closing its doors for good.  Buddy's Rib and Steak has served breakfast and lunch to the community for almost 50 years.
Founder Buddy Hall and his wife sold the restaurant to Phillip Guy in 2010. Guy kept Buddy's legacy alive, but finding people to work became a struggle after the pandemic, forcing him to close the doors sooner rather than later.
"It's been very hectic and busy. Very traumatic for some of my customers. I have had some tears from customers for about 10 days now. I'll probably have some myself. It's been pretty traumatic for Northport, but some of them saw this coming. I need way more to keep the business." Phillip Guy said.
Buddy's Rib and Steak's last day will be June 13. Another business that hasn't been announced yet is set to take up the space soon.

Title_wuva: Veterans Information Fair brings assistance, awareness in Fayette
Description_wuva: TheAlabama State Department of Veterans Affairs,the Montgomery Regional Veterans Affairs Benefits Office, andthe Tuscaloosa VA Medical Centerteamed up to offer veterans in Fayette County and the surrounding areas a town hall discussion and resource fair. It included information booths, a veteran claims clinic, chances to enroll in VA Healthcare, and presentations from each department represented. The purpose of the event was to inform Vietnam War veterans about their potential eligibility for varioushealthcare benefits. Veterans may be eligible for benefits that were previously unavailable since some state and federal laws changed. "We want to get the word out," said Christopher Phillips, veteran service officer. "We want the information to get to our veterans, veterans' families, and surviving family members of veterans are all potentially eligible for benefits." Veterans of the Vietnam War are now entitled to benefits related to hypertension. Phillips said the VA added hypertension as a condition that qualifies veterans for health benefits in Aug. 2022. A Fayette County medical clinic provides vaccinations, treatment, and referrals to the Tuscaloosa VA Medical Center for minor issues that veterans may encounter. Jerry Fulmer, VFW 5406 commander, said the problem is that most veterans in the area are unaware of it. "A lot of veterans don't talk about their service and that is kind of a detriment to their ability to find service," said Fulmer.

Title_wuva: Health Matters: Ozempic
Description_wuva: Type 2 diabetes and weight loss treatment have seen a massive overhaul over the past few years after semaglutide and similar injectable treatments hit the market. Ozempic and Wegovy, which both contain semaglutide, and cousin drugs like Trulicity and Mounjaro are long-term medications that help reduce blood sugar in combination with diet and exercise. University Medical Center Pharmacist Dana Carroll and University Medical Center Registered Dietician Suzanne Henson say Ozempic and drugs like require you to make more changes than simply adding the medication to your routine. "I think there's a common misconception that if I take a medication or what have you, that that's going to fix it for me," Henson said. "We really want to encourage people to start some habits that you may not have tried before. Talk with your doctor, and likely your doctor will talk to you about this what medications you're taking. Will your body use them the same way if you're feeling full on less food? Have a conversation with your physician, don't just run out and purchase it without talking to your physician first." You can watch the full interview below:  For all your primary health care needs, visitUniversity Medical Center, with locations in Tuscaloosa, Northport, Demopolis, Fayette, Carrollton and Livingston.

Title_wuva: Tuscaloosa 2 Tulsa: Two-Step tournament raising money for junior disc golf pair
Description_wuva: TheTuscaloosa Disc Golf Clubwill host theTuscaloosa 2 Tulsa: Two-Step tournamentat Ol Colony Disc Golf Course on Saturday, June 29. The tournament is a way to help two local young disc golfers in their quest to compete in the Junior World Championships in Tulsa, Oklahoma, from July 16 to July 20. Jack Berry and Warren Pate, both 14, are hoping to not only make it to Tulsa but excel when they're there. "I would say it's very exciting, like a 10 out of 10 excitement," Berry said. "I'd say, I'll probably try to play as much as possible and watch footage of the courses that we'll be playing to kind of prepare and maybe try to practice the types of shots that are required on these courses." Both Berry and Pate developed a love and passion for disc golf when they began playing together during the COVID-19 pandemic. "Some of my friends showed me disc golf during the summer of 2020," Pate said. "It was a way that I could see my friends without being worried about spreading any viruses to each other, because, we were outside and in the woods." "It was late 2020, and a bunch of friends and I got into it," Berry said. "Warren (Pate) actually got me into it, and he just kind of showed me how to play. I really enjoyed it and probably the thing that keeps me playing is just getting to see the flight of the disk as it goes into the basket." Berry and Pate are included in a field of 450 junior disc golfers in Tulsa from as many as 40 states and 13 countries. Berry and Pate aren't used to playing competition their age, but they've prepared for this moment and will be ready when the time comes. "Jack and I are the only kids playing really in this community, so I'll play with older people most of the time," Pate said. "I would say I play one round a week. I'm hoping to do to play more than that, but I do have a portable basket in my backyard that I putt on a lot." "That's probably the biggest thought in my mind," Berry said. "There's going to be a lot of kids, and it'll be fun, though, because you can make new friends and see people my age that enjoy playing. I probably go to the course three to four times a week, and then I practice putting my backyard every day or close to it." Although they're good friends and support each other on the course, Berry and Pate will be competing against one another in Tulsa. "Obviously he wants to beat me and I want to beat him," Berry said. "We're cheering for each other to do well because I think we both want to play against each other. We're at our best when we play against each other." "We've been friends before we started playing, so I've never really felt pressure or any anxiety about playing against him," Pate said. Both young men hope that not only the fundraiser, but there performances in Tulsa make waves for disc golf in Tuscaloosa and beyond. They want others to enjoy, participate, and grow the sport they love. "Recreational sports are getting more and more expensive," Pate said. "Go grab discs for $10 at Academy and play a round for free, and you'll be able to play free rounds for a whole year. You don't need to pay $40 every time you play." To participate in the "Tuscaloosa 2 Tulsa: Two-Step" Tournament, visit theirwebsiteto pay and fill out all the required information. The deadline to sign up is Friday, June 28. Hole sponsorships are also available online.

Title_wuva: Update: Woman killed in hit and run Thursday identified
Description_wuva: UPDATE June 14, 3:30 p.m.: The victim has been identified as Patricia Ann Brooks.  The Tuscaloosa Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit is searching for a driver responsible in a fatal hit and run that happened Thursday evening on Englewood Village Drive. Investigators said the woman was struck by a vehicle around 9:30 p.m. Another driver called 911 at 9:32 p.m. and reported he saw a woman in the road. Paramedics attempted life-saving measures, but the victim was pronounced dead at the scene. Officers identified the victim as a 58-year-old woman who lived in the area. After speaking with family members, investigators learned the woman suffered from a medical condition that could have caused her to collapse while walking before she was hit. TPD's Traffic Homicide Unit is working to locate the driver who left the scene. Leaving the scene of an accident with injuries or a fatality is a Class C felony.

Title_wuva: "Nothing lasts forever': Buddy's Rib and Steak closing for good June 13
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Kathryn Mentel Thursday is the last day in business for longtime Northport restaurant staple Buddy's Rib and Steak. After nearly 50 years in business, current owner Phillip Guy made the announcement June 1 that Buddy's is serving its last customers. According to a social media announcement, Guy made several attempts to sell the restaurant to someone who would keep Buddy's Buddy's but no buyer came through. Founder Buddy Hall opened Smalley's Rib and Steak in 1978, later changing the name to Buddy's. He sold it to Guy in 2010. The Guy family said they've been Buddy's lovers for many years, and they're devastated about its impending closure. "It's been great," said Guy's brother Larry Guy. "This has been one of our family's favorite restaurants for years, even when Buddy owned it. We came more often when Phillip bought it, and it brought our family together. For six to seven years, a bunch of us would come to breakfast every Monday. It was a big family get-together every week." After the tradition started, the Guy family lost some of the family members who were part of the tradition, so Buddy's is part of many family memories. Their last Buddy's family breakfast was Tuesday, when 25 people came together to remember the good times. "There's a lot of customers I've met over the years that I didn't know from coming so frequently," Larry Guy said. "I've gotten to know those people. Phillip knows even more people than me." It's a sad day for Northport, as customers who called Buddy's their home away from home will now have to seek out a new spot to call their own. "There are some who come every day for breakfast," Larry Guy said. "It's sad for Northport because they are going to lose this icon and a place for fellowship with friends and family." But Phillip Guy is looking forward to retirement, his brother said. "Nothing lasts forever and all good things come to an end," Larry Guy said. "He's just ready to retire. He's retirement age, and he's ready to move on to a less stressful life." Staffing has been an issue for the business in recent months, and the restaurant has had limited hours. There is currently a deal pending on the building, Larry Guy said, but the family does not know what the buyer has planned.

Title_wuva: What men should know during Men's Health Week
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 Digital Reporter Candace Johnson National Men's Health Weekis June 10 through June 16. University of Alabama College of Community Health Sciences Associate Professor of Internal Medicine Dr. Grier Stewart said this is the time to encourage our fathers, brothers, sons, grandparents or male friends to put their health first. "Men's health is often overlooked, especially in younger men," Stewart said. "It's a recognition of the unique needs of men and their health." Especially as they grow older, it's essential for men to prioritize their health needs. Here are some things men should consider when it comes to their health. If you don't have one already, consider establishing a primary care physician and getting checkups at least once a year. A regular doctor can help catch problems before they reach emergency room-visit levels, especially when it comes to heart health. A prostate screening is a must after 55, but it should be done earlier if you have family members who have had prostate cancer.

Title_wuva: Tuscaloosa's Red Lobster is on the chopping block. If you're a cheddar biscuit fanatic, here's how to make them at home
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 Digital Reporter Candace Johnson Seafood titan Red Lobster has filed for bankruptcy and has effectively startedclosing many locations, including Tuscaloosa's restaurant on McFarland Boulevard. While the restaurant touted its shrimp, lobster and other fresh-from-the-sea goodies, many kept coming back for those beloved, delectably greasy cheddar bay biscuits. Title_wuva: Bright Spots: Nik's Wish helps young adults with cancer have fulfilling experiences
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 Digital Reporter Candace Johnson Fighting cancer is something no one wants to go through, especially younger people. For children with life-threatening diseases, programs like theMake-A-Wish Foundationgive those children and their families a break from the doctors, hospital stays and exhausting treatments. But what about college-aged people who find themselves in the same situation? That's where theNikolas Ritschel Foundationcomes in. The program's namesake, Nikolas Ritschel, had a desire to help people after his own cancer diagnosis at 17. After Nikolas died in 2012, his family ensured that desire would bear fruit. Also known as Nik's Wish, the foundation is focused on bringing joy and encouragement to young adults facing a major cancer diagnosis. Make-A-Wish works with children and many adult-focused wish-granting programs start working with people 25 or older. Nik's Wish is in the middle, focusing on people between 18 and 24. Liz Thompson is an Alabama Wish Angel who holds the program near and dear to her heart after her twin brother Joe faced his own diagnosis. Joe, Liz said, wanted to spend his time helping others and granting wishes until his death in December. Joe was the first Nik's Wish Angel in Alabama, and Liz said her brother's mission has become her own. "Not only do I want to, I feel like I need to carry this on for him," she said. Wish Angels help the organization find donors and grant wishes, and provides support to its beneficiaries throughout their cancer journey. "In the darkest times, we find the most beautiful moments," Liz said. "I think that it helps accepting those things a little bit easier." Joe is a University of Alabama Culverhouse College of Business graduate, and the college is itself giving back by hosting a class in Joe's honor that will work toward granting at least one wish per year. "Even the darkest of times and situations, there is love to see, light to see, and hope to see if we can all just remember that," she said. Title_wvtm: Doctors urging people to stay hydrated during dangerous summer heat
Description_wvtm:
Doctors withAmerican Family Careare urging people to stay hydrated as we head into the weekend and brace for the heat.
Many patients are coming into the clinics with cramps, heat exhaustion, and some feeling lightheaded, according to Chief Medical Officer Dr. LouAnne Giangreco. She is encouraging people to take heat-related illnesses seriously.
"We think we can power through some of these times without making sure we are taking frequent breaks, that we are not taking breaks outside in the heat; making sure we have great sun protection as well if we are in the sun and the heat. Make sure we have appropriate sun protection," Giangreco said.
>>CHECK WEATHERWarmest days of the year: Alabama is heating up just in time for Father's Day
According to theCenters for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC),people who are at the highest risk of heat illnesses include those aged 65 and older, children younger than 2, and people with chronic diseases or mental illness.
Doctors at AFC are encouraging people to ensure they have access to fluids, bottles of water, and fans to battle the heat.
When it comes to heat exhaustion, here are some symptoms to watch out for, according to the CDC: heavy sweating, clammy skin, fast or weak pulse, cramps, and nausea. If you feel like you could be having a heat stroke, seek medical attention.

Title_wuva: Equitable Neighborhoods Initiative celebrates empowering rural residents
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Paislee Roberts TheUniversity of Alabama's Equitable Neighborhoods Initiativehad its milestone celebration Monday. This celebration was to reflect on how far this program has come and how many communities have been impacted. So far, the ENI has helped 20 under-served communities in Alabama receive resources that otherwise would be unavailable. This program prepares local communities for future public health emergencies such as COVID-19. ENI hosts workshops for mental health training, leadership development, and has various youth programs. ENI's focus is on under-served communities in rural areas that do not have these resources available already. "This program has really made a difference. When we go into a community, it is really about empowering the local residents. In a lot of situations, these under-served communities unfortunately are overlooked," said Arturo Menefee, executive director for the UA Center of Economic Development.Â  "We want to make sure we are giving them the special attention they deserve, and we want to help them accomplish their goals." The initial goal was to reach 15,000 people and ENI has exceeded that by reaching nearly 100,000 people.

Title_wuva: 60th anniversary of Bloody Tuesday remembered in Tuscaloosa on Sunday
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Caleb Aguayo First African Baptist Church held a remembrance ceremony and a march to the Tuscaloosa County Courthouse on June 9, the 60th anniversary of Bloody Tuesday in Tuscaloosa. On June 9, 1964, Black protestors led by Rev. T. Y. Rogers hoped to hold a peaceful protest from the church to the county courthouse downtown. Tuscaloosa native Irene Byrd said that morning, peace turned to pandemonium as a white mob descended on the protestors. "For me, it was an eye-awakening experience," she said. "Thinking that you're doing okay, and everything was alright, and all of a sudden to see that up close, first-handedly, was an experience that I'll never forget." Among the mob were police, white citizens and members of the Ku Klux Klan. They beat the protestors back inside of the church by force. "There were people all around this church. Not only policemen, the sheriff, Tuscaloosa police officers, but a lot of clansmen," Byrd said. "With sticks and bats and billy sticks and clubs and cattle prods. You name it, they had it." After arresting Rogers and about 100 protestors, the mob destroyed the church with tear gas and water hoses. In all, 33 people were hospitalized that day. First African Baptist Church choir singers Addisyn and Maddisyn McNealey said remembering the struggle that took place that day is critical for us in the present. "We weren't allowed to go to the courthouse, and I feel like it's very significant for us to understand why this happened, why we're fighting for what we're fighting for, and why we fought for it," Addisyn McNealey said. And 60 years later, the church marched back to the courthouse. This time, the police escorted them there. "So many people sacrificed," said attendee and "Bloody Tuesday" book publisher George Thompson. "The stories have been untold for 60 years, except for a few, in the community. Here's a chance for the public to understand what happened, why it happened, and how we can move forward with a better future." At the Tuscaloosa County Courthouse, Tuscaloosa County Sheriff Ron Abernathy and church leaders addressed the crowd with words of commemoration. And Bloody Tuesday foot soldier Willie Mae Ike Wells said the sacrifices made that day had a ripple effect for generations of Black Americans. "Together, we can do a lot of things if we believe in the cause. And we believed in that cause," Wells said. "We believed that God was on our side. We believed that it was our time; our time had arrived. And it was obvious not only here in Tuscaloosa, but in Birmingham and throughout the South."

Title_wvtm: Widely scattered storms remain in the forecast Sunday
Description_wvtm:
Mild and muggy for Sunday night. Temperatures climb this week with more summer storms for Central Alabama.Check the video forecast for the latest.
Cloud cover will gradually clear overnight after any remaining storms lose their strength this evening. Calm, yet warm and humid will be the story overnight as temperatures settle in the upper 60s and dew points remain elevated.High pressure builds in on Monday leading to a mostly dry and hot day. Morning clouds and patchy fog will be giving way to some sunshine and a warm afternoon. Temperatures climb into the upper 80s to near 90 degrees, with the feels-like temperatures in the low 90s. It will be plenty humid, so a spotty afternoon storm is possible.
Similar to Monday, Tuesday offers another hot afternoon with highs near 90-degrees and a chance for thunderstorms. Better coverage of those may set up north of I-20 and across the Tennessee Valley.
You can plan for increasing coverage of rain and thunderstorms between Wednesday and Thursday across Central Alabama. The 'threats' will be typical of summer storms with heavy rainfall, frequent lightning, hail, and some strong wind gusts all possible.
The meteorological "ring of fire" will set up and send a few waves of strong storms from the Plains to the South between Tuesday and Thursday.
It's very difficult to time these thunderstorm complexes, but should they make it into Alabama, they can carry a risk of strong to severe winds.
Next weekend does not look like a washout but a chance of storms is almost inevitable this time of year with ample amounts of heat and moisture. That being said, a frontal boundary is expected to sweep across Alabama Friday, briefly dropping the humidity for some.
This will be short-lived. Warm and humid weather will quickly make a return with a slim chance of t-storms Saturday and Sunday. You can anticipate highs in the upper 80s, and a generally sunny sky.

Title_wuva: Tuscaloosa Metro Animal Shelter needs your help getting pets into homes
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Paislee Roberts TheTuscaloosa Metro Animal Shelteris running out of space to take in more animals, meaning it needs the community to step up and foster or adopt. Summer means puppies and kittens, and the annual influx alongside the usual animal control drop-offs and owner surrenders are overwhelming area shelters. While there are more than 100 spaces for dogs and around 60 for cats, when there are more animals than there are places to house them Metro doesn't have many options. "We always do everything we can to find room for an animal, but sometimes we have to make hard decisions," said TMAS kennel manager Raquel Kimball. If you're not able to adopt a pet but can open your home on a temporary basis, fostering costs you nothing, Kimball said. Sometimes even a few days away from the shelter can ensure more lives are saved. TMAS gives fosters everything they need to welcome a foster pet into their home: food, crates, litter and medicine if needed. It also offers free training class and anything else you might need while fostering. If you need resources after adoption, Tuscaloosa Metro Animal Shelter recommends theAlabama Spay and Neuter Clinic. The animal shelter offers $20 vouchers to get your pet spayed or neutered if you qualify for financial help. You can apply to foster or adopt an animal by going to theTuscaloosa Metro Animal Shelter's website.

Title_wuva: Bright Spots: Therapeutic Riding of Tuscaloosa offers a unique space for healing
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 Digital Reporter Candace Johnson When you think of animals with jobs, odds are good horses will be a few spots away from the top these days. But atTherapeutic Riding of Tuscaloosa, the equine residents have some major responsibilities. TROT is a place where children and adults, some with disabilities and others with emotional or mental needs, can escape daily life and get a taste of riding, caring for or just being around horses and other animals. It's been a huge benefit for Amelia Adams' daughter Kylie, Adams said. Kylie has autism, and her mother said TROT is a big part of her life. "It helps her with her sensory system," Adams said. "Anything that is gonna make her feel good and is good for her, I want to be a part of." Each of the 30-odd horses at TROT is unique, but Tuff, Patches, Lucy, Lola, Splatt, Moon, Thunder, Soundtrack, Bailey, Rusty and Wyatt are among the friendliest and most involved in therapeutic riding. Many of them have championship racing backgrounds. Nowadays, those champion racers are a lot more focused on the success of their riders than their own speed. Lucy, meanwhile, is a survivor. That's why she's formed a special connection with many children who have lived through abuse or trauma. Licensed psychologist Dr. Marguerite Malone, who's been involved in equine-assisted treatments for more than 30 years and is a leader at TROT, said there's a profound connection between horses and their riders. "Horses adapt to human emotions, changing their heart rate and their respiration rate, according to what's going on with the person near them," said Malone. That means if a child is upset, their horse knows it and can react accordingly. Specially trained therapeutic handlers and mentors ensure horses and their riders get exactly what they need. "We teach them to get control and calm down, and then the horse begins to look calmer and happier," Malone said. TROT's also life-changing for some who work there. Melanie Williams, who's been teaching at TROT for more than a decade, was herself a recipient of therapeutic riding services as a way to help her own neurocognitive and physical ailments. Williams, Malone said, has been dubbed the "heart of the program." The best thing of all, though, Malone said, is seeing how much the program impacts those it serves. "Seeing the same miracle happen over and over for other people is just heartwarming," Malone said. "I am very grateful to be able to do this." If you're interested in learning more about thee program,click right here. Title_wuva: Lake View residents speak out about communal living facility concerns
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Kathryn Mentel Some people who live in Lake View expressed their concern about Broken Vessel residents in a Tuscaloosa County Commission meeting Wednesday. Now Broken Vessel residents share their side of the story. Broken Vessel is a communal living facility located in the Owen Park neighborhood in Lake View. Ryan Harper brought his concerns to the commission meeting. Harper is a resident of the Owen Park neighborhood. "Ever since a year ago, when this place moved in, we've had issues with attempted break ins, harassment and people urinating in our yards," Harper said. Harper said he wants what is best for the people of the facility and the community. "We don't discriminate against the mentally ill, but this is not safe to be in a neighborhood. It needs to be relocated elsewhere. I've spent my whole life advocating for mental health, but you still have to take precautions," Harper said. However, Broken Vessel staff and residents are hurt by the negative comments from the community. "I feel like we should be treated as one. We are people just like them. Yes, we might have some trouble in our life that put us in this situation, but the community needs to understand that this place accepted us when no one else would," said Broken Vessel resident Emily Elkins. Another resident shared her emotional prospective. "They make us feel bad. I thank God for this place that I love so much," said Patricia Sneed, another Broken Vessel resident. Broken Vessel residents say its home to them, and the people of Broken Vessel continue to change them for the better. "Before I came here, I used to feel like I was always alone. Broken Vessel got me out of my shell, and gave me great opportunities," said Tyeshiem Riles, another Broken Vessel resident. Broken Vessel's staff said residents have to meet certain requirements to live in the facility. If they don't meet requirements, then they are told to leave. Residents that have caused issues were removed from the facility. The staff also wants the community to know that they understand both sides of the story, and know what it's like to live in a community and have children to worry about.

Title_wuva: Get ready to roll up your sleeve for the Red Cross
Description_wuva: blood donor, blood donation, blood drive TheAmerican Red Crossis in urgent need of blood and platelet donors. Donations have declined in recent months. According to the Red Cross there were 20,000 fewer blood donations made over the last month than were needed to maintain its blood supply. The decrease is donations is due to several reasons. With that initiative, Red Cross is doing sickle cell trait testing with each time. If you are diversity, you need to know if you have the trait point blank period." The American Red Cross is planning a blood drive at the Red Cross building in Tuscaloosa on June 15.  *

Description_wuva: The National Weather Service in Birmingham has released a statement on the damage during Wednesday's storms. Here is that complete update. Public Information StatementNational Weather Service Birmingham AL504 PM CDT Thu Jun 6 2024 ...NWS Damage Survey for 06/05/24 Tornado Event....Overview... During the evening of June 5, a line of severe thunderstorms entered western Central Alabama from Mississippi, producing areas of wind damage eastward to Interstate 65. Embedded within the line were two EF-1 tornadoes. One began in Itawamba County, Mississippi before dissipating near Bexar in Marion County. The other began in northern Fayette County before tracking through the western and northern parts of Winfield.  .Bexar Tornado...Rating: EF1Estimated Peak Wind: 95 mphPath Length /statute/: 3.38 milesPath Width /maximum/: 300 yardsFatalities: 0Injuries: 0Start Date: 06/05/2024Start Time: 06:43 PM CDTStart Location: 4 WSW Bexar / Itawamba County / MSStart Lat/Lon: 34.1645 / -88.2121End Date: 06/05/2024End Time: 06:48 PM CDTEnd Location: 2 WNW Bexar / Marion County / ALEnd Lat/Lon: 34.201 / -88.1726 Survey Summary:The tornado first touched down in eastern Itawamba County, Mississippi off Pate Rd and traveled northeast across the state line into Marion County, Alabama. Snapped and uprooted trees were observed, consistent with an EF1 tornado. The tornado reached a width of 300 yards as it dissipated along County Highway 94 near Bexar. Special thanks to NWS Memphis for completing this survey. .Winfield Tornado...Rating: EF1Estimated Peak Wind: 95 mphPath Length /statute/: 7.23 milesPath Width /maximum/: 325 yardsFatalities: 0Injuries: 0Start Date: 06/05/2024Start Time: 06:52 PM CDTStart Location: 2 NNE Wayside / Fayette County / ALStart Lat/Lon: 33.8984 / -87.8774End Date: 06/05/2024End Time: 07:01 PM CDTEnd Location: 1 W Tucker / Marion County / ALEnd Lat/Lon: 33.9716 / -87.7897 Survey Summary:An EF1 tornado developed on the northern flank of an MCS, affecting far northern portions of Fayette County and southern portions of Marion County. The tornado initially touched down near Coffee Creek then moved northeast where it crossed Coffee Creek Road and uprooted a few large soft and hardwood trees in the front yard of a residence. The damage was sporadic as the tornado moved through Fayette County producing mostly timber damage as it crossed into Marion County. One home on Atkinson Road sustained minor damage to the vinyl siding. The tornado began to intensify as it approached US HWY 43 to the west of Winfield. Several trees were uprooted and snapped on Pike Road and Pleasant Drive, and a couple of the homes on these roads sustained minor shingle damage, although one tree did fall on a home. As the tornado crossed US HWY 43, it produced minor cosmetic damage to a few of the stores within the Foodland strip mall, and some of the glass doors were blown out. The highest degree of damage was first noted from Silverleaf Road to Rosewood Street where a large concentration of uprooted and snapped trees was observed. Fortunately, structural damage was quite limited in this area despite the amount of tree fall. The tornado continued northeast across State Highway 253 and County Highway 47 where the timber damage once again became more sporadic, consisting mostly of snapped branches and an occasional uprooted softwood. Title_wuva: Health Matters: How Ozempic works
Description_wuva: Type 2 diabetes and weight loss treatment have seen a massive overhaul over the past few years after semaglutide and similar injectable treatments hit the market. Ozempic and Wegovy, which both contain semaglutide, and cousin drugs like Trulicity and Mounjaro are long-term medications that help reduce blood sugar in combination with diet and exercise. University Medical Center Pharmacist Dana Carroll and University Medical Center Registered Dietician Suzanne Henson say Ozempic and drugs like it have been a godsend for those with Type 2 diabetes, but it's also proven effective with weight loss. "Ozempic was originally studied and marketed for diabetes," Carroll said. "And when they saw that those agents could help with weight loss, then the drug companies pursued indications for weight loss." These are known to decrease appetite and reduce food noise in those who take it. Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Zoe Blair The Tuscaloosa City Council voted unanimously Tuesday to schedule a public hearing over the potential revocation of King's Hookah Lounge's business license and put an end to what Tuscaloosa Police Department Chief Brent Blankley has called a "public nuisance." Kansas City Chiefs defensive lineman and former Alabama football player Isaiah Buggs opened King's Hookah Lounge in February 2021. Three years later, the business could be forced to close after several years of what police say is dangerous overcrowding and the city says is a continued issue when it comes to paying taxes and fees. Blankley said there have been issues at the lounge for years, but the past two months have been by far the worst. He sent a letter to the City of Tuscaloosa outlining TPD's challenges with the business. In one major incident April 14, police were called there because of overcrowding reports. When officers cleared out the business, they counted 283 people inside. The lounge has a maximum occupancy of 83. That same night, officers detained Buggs after determining he had two active writs for his arrest with Tuscaloosa Municipal Court. While waiting for confirmation on those writs, police said Buggs became irate and tried to leave. Blankley said he put his hand on Buggs' shoulder, and Buggs shoved him into several other officers. Buggs was taken into custody after that. In the same letter to the council, Blankley said TPD responded to three more calls at the lounge in the 10 days following the April 14 incident. In one of those calls, Buggs and his brother were accused of pointing guns at two of the lounge's patrons. Both were charged with menacing in that incident. Title_wuva: Rural West Alabamians face life-or-death struggles in emergencies as agencies suffer major lack of funding
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Contributor Caleb Aguayo Between decadent, ancient churches and mansions with paint peeling off the walls right across the street from the county hospital in Eutaw sits a small grey house with a blood-red door. Inside, atop hardwood floors with sparse furniture, a team of 20 technicians provides ambulance service to the entire rural area of Greene County from a singular station. "It's like a big wad of Christmas lights," said Greene County EMS Director Chris Jones. "Imagine having to undo that, but they're covered in crap. That's what it feels like sometimes." With four reliable ambulances, three emergency medical technician crews and a boat, the agency is managing Greene County's 911 calls more effectively than ever, said Jones. And it's partially thanks to EMS Board Chair Joe Powell. Jones said response times and the service's availability to handle multiple calls at one time have increased in recent years under Jones' management. But that doesn't mean the organization is keeping up with its expenses, as they far outweigh any incoming income. "It's like a $20,000 per month shortfall," Jones said, though he did not provide a total budget for the service. "We don't know how long we're going to be able to sustain the service," Powell said, noting that a lack of consistent funding for EMS services would eventually lead to a total loss of ambulance services for the county. Greene County's EMS services aren't alone in finding it hard to make ends meet, as many rural areas nationwide are suffering similar issues. The journal EMS-1, using polls from the National Association of Emergency Medical Technicians, said this year thatnational average EMS costs due to EMT wages grewby about 11% and equipment and supplies by about 12% between 2019 and 2022. However, revenues per transport increased by only about 5% in the same time period. According to News 5 Cleveland in 2022, EMS chiefs in Ohio warned thatthe industry was on the verge of collapseat that time. The cause? Underfunding for basic services and increasing costs for maintenance, equipment, staff and supplies. As early as 2019, NBC News notedthe imminent collapse of some EMS services in rural North Dakotabecause of underfunding and staffing concerns. In Alabama, according to a KFF Health News article,NorthStar EMS in Pickens County suffered a substantial loss in fundingsince the closing of the county hospital. And Jones, who regularly works with Pickens County's NorthStar EMS Director Vicky McCrory, said the agency there has struggled to keep its head above the water. "We are funded by insurance, and that's it," McCrory said. "Blue Cross, Medicare, Medicaid." With seven full-time and three part-time employees, McCrory said the agency can't afford to pay competitive wages. A single call puts a crew out of service for up to three hours because of travel times, but she said Pickens County EMTs are doing the best we can with what they've got. "We're losing about $250,000 a year," McCrory said. "We've always been able to maintain ourselves until the last couple of years." The closure of Pickens County's hospital in 2020 directly contributed to those funding shortfalls and increased travel times for the agency's transports. On a busy day, McCrory said, residents in need can wait up to four hours for one of the county's two ambulances to arrive. In Tuscaloosa, NorthStar EMS Director Edgar Calloway said payroll costs between 2020 and 2023 have gone up by nearly 40% while reimbursement for basic services has increase by 10% over the same time. He emphasized that underfunding for basic transport amid mounting costs for the service is a national and statewide issue. "It's not just a problem in the rural areas," Calloway said. "It's a problem nationwide, in urban and rural counties, with governmental agencies, quasi-governmental entities that run through the municipality, whatever. It is a problem everywhere." Jones said the only rural service in Alabama that he knows of that doesn't have major shortfalls is Choctaw EMS in Choctaw County. The reason? Funding provided through property taxes set in the 1980s. In Greene County on the other hand, property taxes equate to about $60,000 a year in revenue. That's less than the organization often spends in a month on payroll alone. Greene County EMS responds to just under 200 calls a month, and Jones said that's a "drop in the bucket" compared with more populated areas. In nearby Tuscaloosa, EMS services respond to about 80 calls a day. While fewer calls means less revenue, the organization is still charged with saving lives. If it goes out of business, residents facing life-or-death emergencies would be left without help when they need it most. The Greene County EMS fleet. In the United States,the median national income as of 2022 was nearly $75,000, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. However, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, EMTsonly make about $40,000 per yearon average in the U.S. But EMS agencies are becoming increasingly unable to pay their workers. The National Rural Health Association noted in a 2018 briefing thatan EMS agency's maintenance leads to "sunk costs,"or investments that cannot be recovered, and a smaller customer base in rural counties results in inconsistent revenue. Because of these lower volumes of calls and large upkeep costs, rural EMS agencies cost more per transport case than their urban counterparts. Longer distances between scattered residents also increases the cost per trip,according to the Rural Health Information Hub. Because of those high costs, RHIhub noted that an increasing number of rural agencies are beginning partnerships with other organizations alongside traditional funding sources so they can keep up with maintenance and payroll costs. The NRHA report said that around 83% of the rural EMS agencies in the study reported multiple funding sources, such as fundraising events or partnerships between private companies and municipal leaders. Among the rural agencies polled, the study noted around 75% of them are funded by counties or local municipalities. Around 60% reported hosting community fundraising events to pay for operations. In addition, most of the rural agencies within the study said they were unsure about the financial feasibility of remaining operational. Greene County is acompletely ruralcounty, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. The bureau's 2021 data saidthe county's median household income is well below averageat around $29,000, compared to Alabama's median income of nearly $60,000. Additionally, the bureau reported that around 35% of working-age adults are employed, compared to the state's employment rate of 56%. Greene County's EMTs travel a web of back roads and interstates to reach any one spot. Source: Alabama Geographic Information Office The U.S. Census Bureau also reported that around40% of the county's population is considered impoverished. With Alabama's poverty rate of just over 16% and theU.S. rate of almost 12%, a large portion of Greene County's residents are unable to pay for health insurance. The bureau reported that whilejust over 8% of the U.S. population is not covered by health insurance, and Alabama sits at around 9%, nearly20% of Greene County residents do not have any coverage. When patients don't have health insurance, EMS agencies have a hard time collecting money for the services they provided, Jones said. Despite the high operating costs and low pay, Greene County EMTs serve nearly 8,000 residents across 640 square miles. That'smore than half the area of Rhode Island, according to the Ocean State's historical webpage. In Greene County, the EMS agency's founder retired in 2019. And after several interim directors came and went, the problems culminated in May 2022 with the resignation of then-interim EMS Director Zac Bolding. In a letter to Alabama State EMS Director Jamie Gray, published by the Greene County Independent on Facebook,Bolding scheduled a suspension of county EMS servicesamid his departure because of the lack of funding. "The impact of having no dedicated EMS response agency for such a large area will have a definite impact on patients experiencing even some of the least complex of medical emergencies," Bolding wrote. According to AL.com,false claims then began circulatingthat Greene County was losing its EMS agency. But Jones, who was an EMT under Bolding at the time of his departure, said he was asked by the EMS Board in Greene County to keep the services functioning. "That started the uphill battle of turning this place around," Jones said. "When I took over, following (Bolding's) exit, a lot of our employees left. So I had maybe six employees including myself to cover ambulance shifts." Part of that uphill battle, Jones said, was logistics. Until he could hire more people, he said he covered 80- to 90-hour shifts a week. It didn't help that at the time the agency had one "good" ambulance, a 1995 model "well in its age," and another "broken down more than it was on the road." Jones said local organizations like the Greene County Sheriff's Office, private donors and towns like Eutaw showed up to help the service's plight. They got money for new ambulances, an all-terrain mini-truck and a small boat for river rescues. To keep up with payroll and maintenance costs, Jones said he has started scheduling transports within nearby counties so the organization can make some extra cash. "Some people might give donations," Powell said, adding that Jones has arranged paid partnerships with local schools and colleges for providing standby EMS at sports games and rodeos. "We don't make money off 911 calls, as sad as it is," Jones said. "The reality is that 911 calls are necessary. They're not what makes money. It's what you've got to do. But dialysis, doctor's appointments, inter-facility transports, those are how ambulance services make their money." But those side jobs won't ever be enough to offset operational costs, he said. "We are hanging on with the stuff we've got, but we have bills to pay like insurance and workman's comp," Powell said. "And it's a hit because we don't get that much from transporting." Eutaw Mayor Latasha Johnson, who's on the EMS board, said, the service's funding is a continued issue, but the county losing its service would be detrimental. "We have been having a problem with financial difficulties, but we are trying to work out a plan to keep it flowing steady," Johnson said. One thing the board is considering is some sort of grant or subsidy. "If we can get a monthly subsidy, it would be a game changer for this service," Jones said. "My dream is to get this service to where we're self-sufficient and don't have to rely on funds from anywhere else." And Powell agreed with Jones on the need for subsidy funding, but he also stressed the need for a cut of the funds from electronic bingo businesses in the county. According to ABC 33/40,local charity bingo propped up Greene County's economyin recent years. The former GreeneTrack bingo hall was the largest employer in the countyuntil its closure amid a pending gambling lawsuit. Several other electronic bingo facilities remain open in Greene County. Signs in support of charity bingo sit in front of the Greene County Jail in Eutaw. Jones and Powell said Greene County Sheriff Jonathan "Joe" Benison collects revenue from the charity gaming halls. And though they said he regularly disperses bingo funds and subsidizes local organizations including Greene County Health Systems and the fire department, Benison only occasionally gives donations to Greene County EMS. It's not consistent, and Jones and Powell said they've asked Benison for steady funding and have thus far been denied. Throwing a larger wrench, though, is that Jones, Powell and Johnson all say no one in the county has received any electronic bingo funds for at least six month. Sheriff Benison did not respond to repeated requests for comment and has made no public statements on the matter since the payments stopped. "We can't point fingers," Johnson said, "because we don't have a set of bylaws for who's responsible for it. But we do know that it belongs to Greene County as a whole. As a mayor, I feel like we're all responsible for the EMS." Greene County Health Systems CEO Dr. Marcia Pugh said Greene County Hospital in Eutaw is also struggling with ballooning costs. "GCH, like other Alabama hospitals, has its financial woes," she said. The health system, which includes the hospital, a nursing home and a clinic, employs around 140 people in total. But like Jones, who noted that insurance companies pay only a portion of the bill, Pugh said the gap between actual costs and insurance reimbursement also affects the hospital's bottom line. "The shortfalls not paid by Medicare, Medicaid and insurance carriers make it difficult to operate," she said. Pugh did not disclose data on the hospital's current funding, but she did speak about issues in Greene County's EMS. "Presently, there is no county or city funding, with few municipalities providing funding assistance," Pugh said. As a fellow member of the Greene County EMS Board, she said she regularly works with Jones to come up with solutions to their organizations' funding concerns. Because of the hospital's funding concerns and inability to transport its own patients, she said losing the county EMS would be "devastating" to its residents. The nearest EMS agency is a 30-minute drive from Eutaw, meaning other areas in the are even farther. "Patients arriving in privately owned vehicles and other ambulance services would be in more distress and require the staff and physicians to treat a much sicker patient," she said. Pugh said Greene County EMS is the only ambulance agency servicing the hospital with ground transport.  In March 2020, funding shortfalls led to the closure of Pickens County Medical Center, which neighbors Greene County. That change has been devastating for Pickens County residents and affects them daily, McCrory and former workers at the hospital said. "Depending on where you are in Pickens County, you could be anywhere from 32 to 50 miles from a hospital," McCrory said. The nearest hospitals to Pickens County are DCH Regional Medical Center in Tuscaloosa and Baptist Memorial Hospital in Columbus, Mississippi. "(Residents) have been dying without the hospital," McCrory said. "It's like we're stuck out here on an island and nobody cares. People are suffering and dying every day, and it doesn't much matter how you beg or plead. We're still where we were a year ago when we started asking for help." Dr. Julia Boothe, a local family practice doctor working at a private clinic called Pickens County Primary Care, said people call or come in "all the time" for spontaneous health care visits requiring a hospital. One incident she remembers happened in late November, when a patient complaining of a cardiac change visited her clinic. When Boothe called the ground EMS and helicopter transport lines, they were all busy and said they couldn't help for several hours. So she drove the patient to the hospital in her personal car and called the cardiologist on the way. That's not a feasible solution. "Some days it's an urgent care," she said. "Some days it's a zoo." Over the years, her practice has added new techniques and equipment so they can handle emergency situations that require stitches, X-rays or short-term IV fluids. "It probably makes no sense to my bottom line," Boothe said. "But you're going to take care of the patients who are in front of you." These financial considerations are also a large reason why doctors are so hard to come by in rural areas. Booth said many health care professionals who work in rural counties are doing so because that's where they came from. "These are the patients they grew up with," she said. "These are their family members." But without the hospital, staying in the area is difficult. Former outpatient clerk for PCMC Cecelia Miller said hospital staff learned of the closure five days beforehand via The Tuscaloosa News. Having worked there for 23 years, Miller said losing the hospital was "like somebody died." She added, "I miss it dearly. We are in need of it because there's nowhere in Pickens County to go." Between 250 and 270 people were laid off when the hospital closed, Miller said, and they lost any compensation for saved-up sick or vacation days. Many people laid off were older and unable to find employment after the closure. "I am a health care worker," Miller said. "I enjoy working with elderly, sick people. But what do you do?" Pickens County needs an emergency room, she said, because it's a space to stabilize patients before they're admitted for full treatment. Without that, lives have been and will continue to be lost. Pickens County Medical Center sits vacant, but the lights are still on and decaying furniture sits within it. "I think that the commissioners, the governor, everybody needs to do their part, look into it, and make sure it happens," Miller said. "It could be some of their relatives that need that attention." Kristen Sanders, a former secretary for PCMC's medical-surgical unit, found herself needing an ambulance on Nov. 8 after her family found her unconscious and unresponsive. Her son performed CPR, and they waited 45 minutes for an ambulance. The trip to Baptist Memorial Hospital in Columbus, Mississippi, was another 45 minutes. The cause of her emergency was a pair of blood clots in her lungs. "(The hospital is) needed not just with elderly people, but with sick people," Sanders said. "And my own experience speaks for itself. Even if it was one of my kids or my friends, it's just scary to not have a hospital close. I'm just thankful that I had help." Dr. Boothe said the problem isn't unique to Pickens County. "We've got to have some directional help, nationally and statewide," Boothe said. "We can't keep saying that this is OK. There's a quality and a level of care that everybody should have access to, and that's what's getting lost in this." In 2022, the Journal of Emergency Medical Servicesoutlined points that could potentially help EMS agenciesamid a funding shortfall. One point suggested counties could combine EMS services and work in a larger geographic area. Jones said Greene County EMS has started working with bordering counties in need of services including Pickens, Marengo and Sumter counties. He's also been speaking with local governments, county sheriff's offices and the Greene County Commission about getting a larger budget. "Two of the towns have been paying into us," Jones said. "But it equals up to about $3,000 a month. I'm very thankful for that, but compared to what we actually need it's a very small portion of that whole picture." District 1 Greene County Commissioner Garria Spencer said the county commission paid for a new ambulance and EMS funding for three months, which amounted to $18,000. Spencer said after EMS got that funding, Jones asked for the county to implement an ad valorem tax. That's a tax residents pay that's earmarked for a specific purpose. "If they want a tax, then they have to do the legwork," Spencer said. He added that the EMS agency should make the community more aware of funding issues before it asks people to pay more taxes. "I just think it's incumbent upon them to present a plan and show these folks what they're going to do with the money," Spencer said. Securing a new ad valorem tax for the agency requires unanimous approval from the county's five district commissioners and a bill passed in the Alabama state legislature. Jones said he hopes for future talks with the county commission and Benison, the sheriff. "I think (the Sheriff's Office) is fixing to restart its (electronic bingo) fund distribution," Jones said. "And they asked for some financial reports that I've given them. So I'm hopeful that this is going to finally turn out to be a fruitful endeavor so we can start getting that kind of revenue. But we need something that's long lasting. Something that's permanent." Facebook Twitter email Linkedin

Title_wuva: Put the phone away: Alabama No. 10 on list of fatal crashes caused by distraction
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Paislee Roberts Alabama ranks in the top 10 for most fatal car crashes because of cellphone distractions,according to research analysis by Florida law firm Anidjar and Levine. But state leaders are hoping to change that statistic. Alabama's Hands-Free Lawwent into effect June 1 and makes driving while holding your cellphone a ticketable offense. "I think the use of hands-free devices is a good thing," said National Road Safety Foundation Director of Public Relations David Reich. "It does seem to reduce crashes, but it is not a total solution. I think that the way to avoid crashes is to focus on what you're doing. Your job is to drive safely and be fully aware of everything around you." Reich said using a Bluetooth receiver so you can speak with a caller through your car's stereo system is helpful but can still cause some distractions. Reich said taking your eyes off the road for three to four seconds while traveling at an average highway speed of 60 or 70 mph is like driving the length of a football field while not paying attention. Reich said he suggests turning your phone off or or giving it to a friend while driving to ensure safety. Alabama's Department of Transportation lists tips to help you go hands-free.They include using Bluetooth, turning on your directions app before beginning your trip, silencing notifications and pulling over and parking if you must use your phone.

Title_wuva: ALEA reports busy Memorial Day weekend with 7 casualties, numerous arrests
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Damaris Epps According to traffic and boating statistics released by Alabama Law Enforcement Agency Secretary Hal Taylor, ALEA is currently investigating seven fatalities that occurred during Memorial Day weekend. Between 12:01 a.m. Friday and midnight Monday, May 27, troopers investigated six traffic deaths in Autauga, Calhoun, Covington, Lauderdale, Marshall and Walker counties. Additionally, ALEA's Marine Patrol Division investigated one boating fatality that happened May 27 on Logan Martin Lake located in St. Clair and Talladega counties. "Our hearts go out to the families and friends of those who lost their lives this weekend," Taylor said in a statement. "These tragedies highlight the need for continued enforcement and public education to prevent such incidents in the future." ALEA made an effort to increase its visibility over the weekend with expanded patrols, driver's license checkpoints, and public awareness campaigns all aimed at diminishing fatalities and injuries. They were busy in the water, issuing 868 Marine Safety Warnings, conducting 740 vessel inspections, 53 vessel assists, and also reaching a new record with 22 Boating Under the Influence arrests in one weekend. The Highway Patrol Department investigated 324 traffic crashes, issued 350 seat belt citations and arrested 29 drivers on DUI charges. Furthermore, ALEA's Aviation Unit along with Gulf Shores and Orange Beach Fire Departments, assisted in the Rescue Swimmer Detail, performing 12 patrol flights and responding to six calls for service: As the busy summer season commences, ALEA reinforces its message to all residents and visitors to stay committed in following traffic and boating regulations, and prioritize safety to prevent future incidents. Title_wuva: Tuscaloosa SAFE Center is looking for donations
Description_wuva: TheTuscaloosa SAFE Centeris in need of donations and they have taken to social media to help the cause. The nonprofit recently posted a need for donations on its Facebook page. The center is in need of items like gift cards for Uber or Lyft, Gatorade or Powerade, bath towels and printer paper. Resources like the ones mentioned above are not covered by grant money the center receives and these gifts are essential for all of their clients, according to the organization. Transporting clients to and from the center is one of their most pressing demands. Gift certificates for Uber or Lyft would make it easier for people to get to the SAFE center, especially those who live outside of Tuscaloosa County. "Because we serve so many counties and a lot of them are rural too, there aren't any taxis out there," Baili Gall, outreach and education coordinator said. "In a lot of rural counties, transportation is an issue in general." The center serves nine counties, including Tuscaloosa, Bibb, Fayette, Lamar, Greene, Hale, Pickens, Sumter, and Marengo. With the majority of customers residing in rural areas, traveling to the center can be challenging for clients who do not have vehicles or other means of transportation.  *
Title_wvtm: Suspect faces 4 counts of attempted murder in April shooting in Tuscaloosa
Description_wvtm:
Authorities continue to investigate an April shooting with multiple victims in Tuscaloosa.
The Tuscaloosa Police Department and the Tuscaloosa Violent Crimes Unit were called to a Texaco gas station at 5400 McFarland Boulevard at about 3:30 p.m. on April 7.
The TVCU originally said three people were shot, allegedly by the same suspect.
After interviewing witnesses, TPD located a suspect who was taken into custody.
All victims survived.
During a follow-up check, the TVCU confirmed Jayhsawn Reed, 27, was charged with four counts of attempted murder.
Court records show Reed has a preliminary hearing set for June 18.

Title_wuva: Get a call while driving? If you don't have a hands-free device, you could get pulled over after June 1
Description_wuva: By WVUA 23 News Reporter Zoe Blair What do you do if your phone rings while you're driving? If you hit accept and put the phone to your ear, you're gonna have to change your ways before that becomes illegal in Alabama June 1. The new hands-free law makes it illegal to hold your phone for any reason, whether it's talking, texting, finding a new Spotify playlist or glancing at your map app. Alabama Law Enforcement Agency State Trooper Cpl. Reginal King said distracted driving is a real and potentially deadly issue. And getting distracted is easy. "We see a lot of different forms of distracted driving," King said. "Typically, when we say distracted driving, cellphones are first things that come to mind. It's important to know that there are so many other ways to get distracted. Changing the radio, grooming yourself, drinking a beverage or even turning around to check on your kids can be distracting." You can touch your phone to answer a call and put it on speaker, but you can't keep it in your hand. So if you don't have a car mount for your phone, it might be time to get one. The law, passed in 2023, has been getting enforced under a one-year grace period. That meant anyone pulled over for violating the law got a written warning. But starting Saturday, you'll be getting a citation. Just like seat belt laws, it's a secondary offense charge. That means you can't be pulled over just because you're caught with a phone to your ear, but if you were speeding you're gonna be facing a ticket for both actions. Here's the penalties: If you're worried about how those points will affect your driving record, you can check out the rules on thatright here. King said State Troopers see far too many crashes caused by distracted driving, but they're hoping this law can put a dent in them. "Any time you're operating a motor vehicle if you receive a phone call and can't go hands free, it's always best to wait," King said. "Pull on the side of the road or wait until you get to your destination to answer that call or respond to that text. There is never a text out there that's going to be more important than staying safe or staying alive." First offense: $50 fine and one point on your driver's record Second offense: $100 fine and two points
Title_wvtm: A new Alabama law going into effect could fine you for driving with a phone in your hand
Description_wvtm:
A new Alabama hands-free law will be enforced this month, meaning people will be fined for having their cell phones in their hands while driving.
Many in the state believe this law will help reduce accidents on the road.
In Alabama, about 1800 crashes occurred as a result of distracted driving by the use of cell phones in 2020, and about 1900 crashes in 2019.
>> THE LATEST:Headlines and weather from WVTM 13
The Alabama Legislature enacted the hands-free law in 2023 to address the rising accidents caused by distracted drivers. This year, if someone is distracted by their cell phones while driving, this could result in fines starting at $50.
Individuals will also receive points on their driving record.
The Alabama Law Enforcement Agency will begin enforcing Alabama’s New Hands-Free Law beginning at 12:01 a.m. on Saturday, June 15, 2024.

Title_wuva: Vance mayor orders speed restrictions in Briar Ridge subdivision
Description_wuva: VANCE- The Colburn family of the Briar Ridge subdivision were the proud owners of their dog, Dolly. On April, 20, while the family was playing in their front yard, Dolly ran into the road and was struck by a driver traveling through the neighborhood at high speeds. "I was working in the backyard but my children, wife, and around eight kids were in the front yard running back and forth stop sign stop sign racing their bicycles," Josh Colburn said. "Then I heard screaming and yelling from the front yard. I just thought the kids were playing but I heard the screaming again and then I took off to find my dog lying over in the neighbor's yard just kind of flopping around because she had just been hit by a car." Unfortunately, Dolly didn't survive the accident leaving family members saddened and angry. This wasn't the first time Colburn or other residents noticed vehicles traveling at unnecessarily high speeds through Briar Ridge. The subdivision has no speed bumps, rumble strips, or a posted speed limit. "We've seen people flying by around 60 to 65 miles an hour," Colburn said. "Our neighborhood should be around 15 miles an hour. We've also had other issues where people have been doing burnouts and donuts in our neighborhood." Once residents heard about the accident involving Dolly, they decided to meet as a neighborhood to discuss potential resolutions for the speeding issue. The neighborhood decided they wanted to propose the addition of speed bumps in the subdivision to the Vance City Council at their weekly meetings. Over 70 Briar Ridge residents signed a petition supporting that resolution. However, Colburn and others were greeted with a different viewpoint from Vance Mayor, Brenda Morrison. "I sent her (Morrison) an email suggesting that we have speed bumps put it in the neighborhood," Colburn said. "When she called me, her response to these speed bumps was speed bumps weren't the solution. Speed bumps were a hazard themselves because they could cause damage to people's vehicles or people could lose control of their vehicles and possibly drive into someone's home. When she said that, I was dumbfounded. I was like well the common sense thing is that speed bumps are supposed to stop you from speeding. If you're not speeding or flying through the neighborhood when you go over these speed bumps, then you're not going to take a chance in damaging your vehicle or running into someone's house. I'd rather someone damage their vehicle than kill an animal or kill a kid God forbid." In a statement to WVUA 23 Digital, Morrison explained what the city of Vance's solution would be for Briar Ridge's speeding issue. "We have ordered speed limit signs to go within the subdivision," Morrison said. "Also, we plan to put down some rumble strips. To put down the rumble strips, the weather has to be a lot hotter than it is." While it's not the exact resolution they wanted, Morrison and the city of Vance is making an effort to resolve the problem. Colburn and other residents have also noticed the uptake in police surveillance since the airing of their grievance. Only time will tell whether these speed limit postings or rumble strips make a difference in the speeding issue. If nothing else, Colburn hopes drivers will slow down and pay attention when driving through any subdivision because you never know what could be in the road. "Our dog wasn't wasn't just a dog, she was a family member," Colburn said. "She was our daughter; she was a part of the family. She was my son's best friend and I just want to see something done in the neighborhood to stop the speeding, to stop the reckless driving in our neighborhood before a child gets hurt or killed. God forbid that happens."
